text: You already know that hyperparameters are settings you choose before training. Finding good ones means trying many, and SageMaker automates that as a tuning job.

A tuning job needs four things. Ranges for each setting you want searched: integer, continuous, or a list of categories. One objective metric, and for your own script that metric is pulled out of the training log with a regular expression. A strategy, which decides how each next candidate is chosen. And a budget: how many training jobs in total, and how many may run at once. Every candidate is a full training job, so the budget is also your cost limit.

Here is the same idea run locally. I looped over eight random settings, ran the same training script each time, and extracted the accuracy with the same regular expression I would give SageMaker. Deep trees overfit this noisy data, and the best result, about sixty-seven percent, came from a shallow forest of two hundred thirty-four trees.

In the current SDK, illustrative and not run here, a HyperparameterTuner wraps the trainer from lesson nine. You pass the objective metric name, the ranges, the metric definitions, a strategy, and your limits, then call tune. Version two had the same idea with an estimator.

Four strategies. Random search ignores past results, so running many jobs in parallel does not hurt it. Bayesian optimization uses everything learned so far to pick the next candidate, and it is the default. Grid search tries every combination, but only for categorical values. And Hyperband suits iterative models like neural networks, stopping weak jobs early.

When the job finishes, ask the tuner for its best training job, and pull the analytics table. It has one row per job with its settings and final metric, so you can see how each setting behaves and narrow the ranges for a second, tighter search.
Dozens of jobs means dozens of results to keep straight. Lesson twelve is about experiments and model tracking.
